uff. One of those games where I sincerely doubt the developers played it themselves.
The relatively untouched setting and 2,5-D-perspective is already the most positiv-ish one can say about Pharaonic. Visually/creatively bland, basically only two types of enemies copypasted endlessly (light and heavy - even most bosses are just an iteration of one), painfully slow combat (hit-hit-wait for enemy attack-dodge and repeat for the overly long healthbar), every movement feels like being underwater, nonsensical and inconsistent hitboxes and -detection (for the player as well as the enemies), grindy leveling and so forth.
Was even to boring for killing the time while waiting in the hospital bed. Runs well enough on the Deck at least.

Judging from the other reviews, this is a highly underrated game; sure enough bringing souls-like mechanics to a 2Dish environment could feel strange, however the gameplay is curated and well-thought, with many and diverse weapons, skills, rings, spells, enemies, boss fights and maps. On top of this, truly great settings, great egyptian vibes with many references to their cult and religion. Great sound design as well. Story is also good. I also very much appreciated that enemies' gender is randomly chosen.

I had already played it back on PS4 but had to get it again for PC. I still think this game is a lot of fun and underrated. A very well done, challenging 2.5D Souls-like game with a fresh setting. I also like the art style a lot. Not the most demanding graphics, but it just feels nostalgic in a good way, a bit like fun PS2 games in prettier. I would wish the devs would return to this game some day and make a second one in the series. Great fun!

Pharonic, a visually delicious dedicated combat based Egyptian themed Hack and Slash and in my opinion a very underrated game in the Souls Like genre.  

Control Responsiveness is perfect.  Combat is based on stamina and frankly if you don't know how to manage your stamina in Pharonic then yes you will criticize control responsiveness as no combat action may occur without stamina and yes you will get beaten to a pulp.  The interface has a stamina bar which must be monitored constantly in order to optimize your next move.

Weapons and Armors are plentiful and associated stats do make a difference, a huge difference as Pharonic is a stamina based game.  You will not necessarily use the best weapon found or the best armor found.  You must be strategic in your loadout to match your style of play.  Weapons, armor, magic implements and attribute boosting rings must be carefully and thoughtfully selected.

Pharonic is a pseudo 2.5D game.  Combat takes place on two dimensional plane but exploration allows movement around a 3D map.  For this reason alone Pharonic is extremely unique and movement in this regard is well executed.  However, implementation conflicts with the game's static maps which I will subsequently address.  You are not locked in to any one direction.  The game is certainly not open world but you do have freedom of movement to a degree.

The in game map objectively speaking leaves much to be desired.  The maps are static and there are no location pointers identifying where you are on the level.  Levels rotate but as stated maps are static so new players will have difficulty identifying locations.  There is a strategy guide at trueachievements which mitigates map issues.  Eventually you will become "Pharonic map literate".   The map issue will primarily affect the user experience on the earlier levels.   Subsequently as you learn stage layouts navigation will be simple.

Though I submit that I have no knowledge of the game's inner workings each of the many stages has it's starting skill level set based on the user's skill level upon entry.   Once a stage level is set the stage skill level does not reset under any circumstance.  Therefore you can grind to level up within the stage but don't have to.  Going back to early stages to "mop up" achievements and so forth confirms this.  Inherently there is some repetition involved as map enemy encounters are reset under several conditions.  

1) Saving the game which can be done on each stage at shrines. 
2) On death you are resuscitated with full health and mana.  
3) Starting the game on any level.

Repetition in Pharonic is going to be an acquired taste but in reality it's no different than many games in other genres.  The claim that you have to fight already fought enemies is mostly false.  The game is designed so that many enemies already encountered may be bypassed.  There are battles that are force locked or gated within a 2D arena.   These battles are not skippable and represent usually the most challenging within the stage.  The developers therefore have struck a nice balance between enemy non-repetitive and repetitive encounters enabling stage advancement by making the player work for their progression.

Enemies are varied enough and very well designed.  Many have multiple move-sets which you will be required to master or at least be able to recognize.  Bosses are very varied in design and each stage has one.  Some are more challenging than others.  For the many enemies throughout the game you will have to adjust your loadouts to either go for more stamina but less offense and / or protection or less stamina but more offense and / or protection.  

Combat scenarios evolve from the mundane 1 vs 1 encounters to multiple concurrent enemies and this is where the difficult especially ramps up.  Here the 2D combat plane has weaknesses.  Occasionally there might be an enemy that executes a special charge move from off the screen.  Two enemies may attack milliseconds apart making defense and stamina management very difficult as when you execute a shield block, the block is only successful if you have not depleted stamina.  As a result you'll take damage when enemy offense overwhelms your stamina meter.  Finally, within gated arenas damage avoidance may be very difficult when cornered (to this I say don't get cornered :p).  Thankfully I'll categorize these "faults" as nitpicks and with mastery of the game they will not be much of a problem.  I thoroughly enjoyed the combat in Pharonic and many times seeking out to re-play difficult scenarios.

There is an element of magic involved and in my opinion (it is my review :p) the implementation is perfect.  As a plebe you start out with very little health and mana but these attributes vastly increase as you level.  Mana cannot be regenerated (at fountains) once used.  Mana however, as health can be replenished at shrines.  There are many magic implementations to be acquired and chosen throughout the game.  Selection and usage must be properly managed.  Mana allocation is not too much where magic dominates the game but it's there for combat support.  Playing the game through to the end I've come to appreciate the developer implementation. 

Pharonic can be played with a controller or mouse and k/b.  Both methods of input are completely re-mappable.

Pharonic is an underrated gem with great combat.  A very challenging entry and one worth your time assuming you're up for a serious challenge.

Pharaonic is a challenging action role-playing game that draws clear inspiration from the Soulslike formula while carving out a strong identity through its Ancient Egyptian setting and side-scrolling perspective. Developed and published by Milkstone Studios, the game places players in a harsh, myth-infused world where divine authority and human suffering are deeply intertwined. From the outset, it establishes a grim and oppressive tone, presenting a land ruled by a tyrant known as the Red Pharaoh, whose reign has twisted both mortals and gods into instruments of cruelty. Rather than offering comfort or power fantasies, Pharaonic emphasizes struggle, perseverance, and the slow accumulation of skill and knowledge.

The journey begins with the player as a prisoner who escapes captivity and is thrust into a sprawling, interconnected world filled with danger at every turn. Although the game is presented in a 2.5D side-scrolling format, the world design is anything but simple. Regions interlink through branching paths, hidden shortcuts, and optional areas that reward careful exploration. Progress often involves unlocking new routes that loop back on themselves, gradually building a mental map of the land. This structure encourages curiosity while maintaining a sense of constant risk, as even familiar paths can become deadly if approached carelessly.

Combat is the defining feature of Pharaonic and demands patience, precision, and respect for enemy patterns. Battles are slow and deliberate, with stamina management playing a central role in every encounter. Blocking, parrying, dodging, and striking must be carefully timed, as reckless aggression is swiftly punished. Enemies hit hard, and even common foes can be lethal if underestimated. Boss fights, in particular, serve as intense skill checks that test mastery of the game’s mechanics, often requiring multiple attempts to learn attack patterns and openings. Victory feels genuinely earned, while defeat becomes part of the learning process rather than a simple setback.

Character progression adds meaningful depth to the experience. Throughout the adventure, players collect weapons, shields, armor, and accessories that significantly affect combat style and survivability. Equipment choices matter, influencing stamina usage, defense, and offensive capabilities. Lighter builds allow for quicker movement and dodging, while heavier gear provides protection at the cost of agility. In addition to physical gear, the game introduces divine powers and magical abilities that further expand tactical options, allowing players to adapt their approach based on personal preference and situational demands.

Visually, Pharaonic distinguishes itself through a stylized interpretation of Ancient Egypt that blends historical motifs with dark fantasy elements. Hieroglyph-inspired designs, monumental architecture, desert landscapes, and mythological creatures create a setting that feels both exotic and oppressive. The art direction emphasizes scale and menace, particularly in boss encounters where towering figures loom over the player. Sound design and music reinforce the atmosphere, using ominous tones and subtle ambient effects to heighten tension and underscore the sense of an unforgiving world shaped by divine wrath.

Storytelling in Pharaonic is understated and environmental rather than overt. Instead of lengthy cutscenes or constant exposition, the narrative unfolds through NPC interactions, item descriptions, and the visual language of the world itself. Players piece together the history of the Red Pharaoh’s rule and the role of the gods by paying attention to small details scattered throughout the environment. This fragmented approach complements the game’s themes, making the story feel like a mystery uncovered through persistence and observation rather than something explicitly handed to the player.

While the game’s difficulty and deliberate pacing will not appeal to everyone, they are central to its identity. The learning curve is steep, and repetition is often necessary, which can be discouraging for players seeking a more forgiving or fast-paced experience. Some enemy encounters and areas may feel repetitive over long sessions, but this is largely offset by the satisfaction that comes from mastery and progression. The game is clearly designed for players who enjoy methodical combat and the sense of accomplishment that comes from overcoming seemingly insurmountable odds.

In the end, Pharaonic stands as a distinctive and ambitious entry in the action RPG genre. By merging Soulslike combat principles with a side-scrolling format and a richly stylized Ancient Egyptian setting, it offers an experience that feels both familiar and refreshingly different. It rewards patience, observation, and adaptability, delivering a journey where every victory is hard-won and every mistake carries weight. For players drawn to challenging combat, atmospheric world-building, and deep mechanical engagement, Pharaonic provides a demanding but ultimately rewarding adventure through a land ruled by gods and tyranny.

Да вот только здесь встают ещё два "креативнейших" решения: не давать игроку переходить между лестницами и проходами в другие сегменты уровня, когда рядом враги, и засады. При первом решении приходится постоянно, повторяю, постоянно играть в перегонку врагов с одного конца пути на другой, чтобы банально перейти через лестницу. В качестве примера возьму опять Аварис, и те, кто там был, скорее всего поймут, почему. Почему? При втором случае вам сама игра запретит перейти дальше, если вы не отобьётесь от волны врагов. Особенно больно вы это почувствуете в Фивах и самом храме, в котором вам буквально закидывают четырёх врагов, которые, на минуточку, атакуют одновременно, что просто не дает вам времени дать отпор. Не буду врать, я сам дропнул игру, когда пытался пройти через очередную засаду там. Камон, я даже один из сундуков пропустил из-за того, что надо было опять пройти засаду. Плюсом к этому добавляем ранее перечисленные 4 врага за засаду одновременно и получаем сожженое седалище вашей табуретки.   Какой итог из всего вышенаписанного обзора? Не играйте в эту игру. Это максимально душная и унылая ходилка-бродилка, не стоящая своего времени. [h2]Pharaonic, a review in 2025[/h2]

It’s a bit late to write this review, but it might still be useful for someone interested in this game in 2025. This 2.5D action/soulslike game, set in ancient Egypt, has some notable strengths but is hindered by several issues that prevent it from reaching its full potential.

After three playthroughs to experiment and unlock all achievements, here are my thoughts:

[h3]Pros[/h3] [list] [*][b]Visually Striking Setting[/b]: The combination of the art style and ancient Egyptian theme is immersive and captivating. [*][b]Solid 1v1 Combat[/b]: Combat in one-on-one encounters feels responsive and satisfying. [*][b]Varied Combat Mechanics[/b]: Attacks can be parried, blocked, or dodged, adding some variety and skill to the combat system. However, this could have been explored further. [*][b]Decent Item Variety[/b]: For a short game, there’s a good amount of gear and items to discover. [*][b]Fun Moments[/b]: At its best, the game “clicks” and delivers genuinely enjoyable gameplay. [*][b]Traps[/b]: Certain environmental traps allow you to outsmart enemies, dealing significant damage. I’d have loved more of these interactive elements. [/list]

[h3]Cons[/h3] [list] [*][b]Cryptic Item Descriptions[/b]: Item descriptions are often vague, making their purpose and their specific stat boosts unclear. [*][b]Repetitive Builds[/b]: Despite encouraging diverse builds with light/heavy weapons and armor, most builds feel similar, boiling down to managing stamina for attack strings, dodging, blocking, or parrying. [*][b]Lackluster Packs[/b]: Packs (abilities) are disappointing, with only stamina regeneration or damage-boosting packs feeling really viable. [*][b]Unbalanced Weapons[/b]: Some light weapons shine with fast, powerful attack spam (e.g., R2 movesets), making them highly effective after a dodge with a stamina pack. Heavy weapons, however, feel sluggish, exposing you to risk against dodging enemies, and no heavy weapon felt rewarding enough to justify its slow swings. [*][b]Inconsistent Level Design[/b]: Simple layouts work well, but some areas, like the [i]Crystal Caves[/i], are frustratingly maze-like. Doors teleport you unpredictably, making navigation confusing. Simpler, cohesive exploration would have been better. [*][b]Poor Map System[/b]: The map is nearly useless and would’ve been better omitted. [*][b]Awkward Gank Fights[/b]: Multi-enemy encounters feel clunky. Enemies line up to attack, sometimes throwing out-of-range hits that chain into hard-to-escape combos. Rolling through enemies often leads to punishment, forcing you to accept unavoidable damage and focus on trading blows. [*][b]Untactical Bosses[/b]: Boss fights lack the tactical depth expected given the player’s movement options. [*][b]Unrewarding Parries[/b]: Parrying doesn’t feel impactful. A full stamina regeneration after a successful parry would have made it more rewarding without being overpowered. [*][b]Clunky Heavy Builds[/b]: Heavy weapon + heavy armor combos are underwhelming. Enemies dodge heavy swings easily, draining stamina and leaving you vulnerable. Blocking with heavy shields to set up attacks feels slow and tedious, though parrying helps land a hit during enemy recovery. [*][b]Flat Leveling System[/b]: The leveling system lacks depth, making progression feel uninspired. [/list]

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3] While the cons outweigh the pros, there are moments when the game’s simplicity and combat shine, delivering fun and engaging gameplay. Unfortunately, it often feels [i]clunky[/i], [i]messy[/i], and lacking in variety. A greater focus on tactical 1v1 or 2v1 combat, with more movement options, unique weapon movesets, and compact, polished level design, could have elevated this game significantly.

[h3]Score[/h3] [b]5.5/10[/b]

Pharaonic is a game bogged down by repetitive gameplay and lack of meaningful progression. From the very beginning, the combat shows little evolution, and players will quickly notice that the same types of enemies are constantly being reused. The enemies are mostly humanoid warriors wielding various weapons, and even the bosses are essentially larger versions of regular foes with bigger weapons. This makes the game feel monotonous, and the leveling system is rendered pointless as enemies level up with you, providing no real sense of growth.

The combat itself is a slog, with most enemies having too much health, making grinding feel unbearable due to the repetitiveness of encounters. Traversing the game world is also a confusing experience. Despite being on a 2D plane, the environments weave between the foreground and background, making it difficult to navigate. Traps scattered throughout the levels can easily cripple a run, adding frustration rather than challenge. While maps can be purchased, they do little to help orient the player, as understanding your position on them is not intuitive.

The setting is one of the few redeeming aspects of Pharaonic, as games set in ancient Egypt are rare. However, the novelty of the setting is not enough to overcome the dull gameplay. The game also pushes players to interact with background NPCs to obtain items needed for progression, which constantly disrupts the game flow. With uninteresting writing, these interactions feel like a chore rather than a rewarding part of the experience.

Overall, Pharaonic struggles to provide engaging content, and while the setting is unique, it isn’t enough to make up for the repetitive combat, frustrating navigation, and lackluster progression.

Adéntrate en el misterioso antiguo Egipto, donde probablemente pasarás más tiempo en el limbo que cualquier alma en duelo! Pharaonic es un RPG de acción algo peculiar, donde tu misión principal, además de salvar el mundo, es no apagar la consola/computadora de la frustración.

I haven't played too many Souslikes, but this one is by far my favorite. It was so addicting I played it three times in a row and got every achievement! It's not a flawless game though, which I detail down below in my quick guide to gittin' gud at it.

First, you're gonna wanna pick which four of the game's eight skills you want to focus on, because you can't max them all out in one playthrough. You get 22 skill-ups (two of which are missable), and each skill can be leveled five times. The skills come in pairs, so you'll be picking one sibling per pair and sticking with it. Unfortunately, the game does have objectively better choices, and here they are:

Light Weapons over Heavy Weapons - Heavy weapons take too much stamina to comfortably use. The only benefit to them is the assortment of spears (long reach), but you can get a light spear as a drop from the green sahuagin, the Fishneedle, which is the best weapon in the game.

Small Shields over Great Shields - Don't let the higher damage reduction fool you. You won't be taking shields to be a tank; you'll be taking them to block the undodgeable (blue) attacks, and DODGING everything else. Learning to dodge in place is the key to mastering this game, but the blue attacks require a shield. Trying to block with a Great Shield runs the risk of your stamina being emptied, guard-breaking you and leaving you open. Light shields with high Swiftness will prevent that.

Heavy Armor over Light Armor - The weight of your armor reduces your max stamina, but the penalty is SO negligible at all points in the game, that there's no reason not to take the defensive option. It doesn't slow you down or encumber you to wear it, so tank up.

Support Backpacks over Offensive Backpacks - The offensive spells in this game suck ass. Most are single-shot projectiles of varying strength, and the other makes a patch of fire on the ground that hurts everything on contact, including YOU. Support spells are just the best, affording you increased weapon damage, defense, health regeneration, etc.

So there you go. Heavy Armor, Small Shields, Light Weapons (Fishneedle), and Support Backpacks. Save all your skill-ups for those and you'll breeze through this game. Also, remap your controls! The default setup will confuse seasoned Souls-players.

Next are some cool tricks I learned.

-If you leave an area, either by walking or warping, fountains will refill, but most enemies won't respawn. If you get low on health, just warp to Set Maat, use its fountain, warp back, and continue. Or walk outside and use the local fountains.

-You only get three uses of your canteen, but the Ring of Shedet gives you a fourth at the cost of reduced healing. A net loss, mathematically, BUT... If you take the Ring OFF after your first sip, your remaining sips will regain their strength.

-Quitting the game functions like a Homeward Bone. Very useful for warping around or avoiding death so you don't drop your XP.

-You can break through enemy shields by parrying them. I didn't know this was a thing til after I platinum'd the whole game...

Anyway, I love this game. 9/10

Pharaonic is a game that, while attempting to emulate Dark Souls in many respects, fails to replicate the best things about it. Players take on the role of Dagi, a prisoner seeking to escape from prison and uncover the truth about The Red Pharaoh. While the plot is fairly basic, the game's focus is primarily on combat. The game's art direction is exceptional, with detailed backdrops that is occasionally lacking in visual variety. The game's environmental storytelling is also lacking, with players killing enemies with a minimal sense of purpose or exploration. While the game tries to emulate Dark Soul’s vagueness to create a sense of intrigue, it ultimately falls short by missing the purpose of why that worked in the first place.

Pharaonic offers a wide variety of weapons, with each weapon having unique advantages and disadvantages against different enemy types. Players acquire weapons and armor from enemy loot, merchants, and treasure chests. Equipment falls under two categories: light and heavy, where the former increases speed but decreases protection, and the latter offers more protection but less speed. The game's upgrade system allows players to increase their equipment level by finding Shabti gems, buying from merchants, or completing side quests. Trainers offer to increase equipment skills in exchange for a Shabti gem. Pharaonic offers a wide variety of weapons, including short swords, spears, and maces, each with unique advantages and disadvantages against different enemy types. Boss battles can be challenging, requiring players to hone their strengths and learn the weaknesses of each boss.

Pharaonic's gameplay is engaging but flawed, with enemies acting as damage sponges that take an unreasonable amount of hits to kill. The lack of damage scaling leaves players with few effective options on improving their offensive capabilities, leading to heavy weapons being the obvious choice. Shields, on the other hand, are problematic because most of them do not block 100% of damage and often consume more stamina than their Dark Souls equivalents. Moreover, enemies tend to attack in mobs, often overlapping each other and executing a mix of unblockable and undodgeable attacks, making it difficult to avoid damage. The absence of a sprint button and the naturally slower combat movement further exacerbate the issue, leading to inevitable damage at times.

In conclusion, Pharaonic falls a little too short of its Dark Souls inspirations. The game's art direction and environment design are extremely well done and are pleasant to look at, but are undermined by a lack of substance in plot and NPCs. Essentially this game boils down to just combat, which as previously stated is problematic. Finally, the ending to the game is abrupt, short on details, and doesn’t lead to a NG+; it’s just over.

Sometimes you come across little known games on Steam with little recognition and it catch you by surprise. Pharaonic is one of those titles. A true hidden gem action adventure game with Souls-like combat and mechanics. If you like Egyptian mythology and From Software games I'm confident that you will get enjoyment out of this.

And before I forget it is a joy to play on Steam Deck. 9/10!

O Pai e a mãe de Dark Souls brigaram e ai o Pai foi no Egito e meteu um filho. 
PHARAONIC. 

Bebe na fonte da dificuldade e inimigos gigantes, um personagem com motivações para lutar e ataques fracos e fortes a usar; o  jogo pega essa premissa de combate simples e força você a situações difíceis, por meio de posicionamentos de inimigos e armadilhas ambientais. O que isso significa é que é mais do que provável que você morra muito aqui. Assim como em um jogo Souls , quando você morre, você deixa sua experiência para trás, e se você puder voltar lá sem morrer novamente, você pode coletar sua experiência. Uma vez que a grande diferença neste jogo é que você automaticamente sobe de nível depois de coletar experiência suficiente, e você não precisa viajar para a fogueira mais próxima.

As armas variam de enormes cutelos improváveis ​​a espadas mais curtas e mais manejáveis, e as armaduras se destacam visualmente umas das outras. Cada item afeta seu peso e resistência, e você precisará tomar suas próprias decisões sobre como deseja jogar. É realmente um sistema flexível, tomando a liderança da série Souls , mas simplificando-o para ser mais acessível e tentar compensar um pouco mais o jogador na sua experiência com Pharaonic.

Os mapas do game serão um grande e longo vai e traz de itens e vai e volta até enjoar, mais é tudo um sistema para fortificar o seu sistema 2D, onde a câmera conseguirá esconder: atalhos, baús e armadilhas. 
Mais por outro lado, por usar esse mesmo sistema 2D, muitos encontros com inimigos no caminho não poderão ser evitados e nem contornados, o que pode vir a gerar uma certa sensação de repetitividade e chatisse na gameplay,

Pros / What's good?
----------------------------------------
 The Egyptian theme is an eye-pleasing hook, and consistent throughout most of the game. The Serket armor set looks like something from monster hunter and the Ishtar set has this silly blue-pink paint job going on.

 Combat is challenging, tactical almost. To  Some attacks cannot be blocked, only dodged. Some cannot be dodged, only blocked. These attacks have 'colored trails' on them: red is unblockable, blue is undodgeable. Parrying - I found it new that you could parry enemies blocking with their shield in order to get them to drop their guard.

You compliment your weapons with tablets, which go into the 'backpack' slot. Two varieties: Support and Offense. Support gives a temporary buff, Offense delivers a magical attack.

People are quick to make this game out to be "Egyptian Dark Souls". I think the only real soulslike thing about it is that when you die, you leave behind an orb (you only lose xp on death). Collecting the orb gives you your xp back. There are 3 stats- health, stamina, and ka (ie mana). Leveling up increases these stats by a certain amount.
 
Cons/ What could be better?
------------------------------------------------------------
 Item Descriptions. Quite a few are vague/ misleading. For example:
1. Tablet of Blessings: "You can already feel your stamina increasing!" Does not increase stamina. It rapidly regenerates stamina while active.
2. Ring of Tjuiay: Mentions a smuggler that survived many deadly attacks, thanks to this ring. Does not give you a 'saving grace' of leaving you with a sliver of hp when hit with a lethal attack. Gives you  10 points of defense.
3. Ring of Tawosre: You can pick this ring up about halfway through the game. I beat the game without finding out what it does. The description talks of a general who was deadly with a sword, occaissonally killing with a single blow. But this game doesn't have ripostes /crits /attack weak spot for massive damage. According to a forum post from a dev, it just increases damage.
4. Pyramidskin: The lvl 4 support tablet's description gives the impression that it gives you temporary invincibility. I found out the hard way it does not.
 Shields have a stat called 'swiftness'. What does this measure? Movement speed? Nope. The time it takes to bring the shield up? Nope. Parrying speed? Nope. It measures how much stamina is lost/ kept when you successfully block. The higher it is, the better.

 The way defense stat works in this game is weird. It's not a direct damage threshold or percentage. It's....'proportional'? According to a dev: (assuming enemy deals 100 damage)
"Against an armor of 100 (Level 1 Light Armor), actual damage is 100.
Against an armor of 120 (Level 0 Heavy Armor), actual damage is ~95.
Against an armor of 55 (Level 0 Light Armor), actual damage is 125."

In combat you cannot manually make your guy face a certain direction. You'll automatically face the closest enemy. you may be able to dodge attacks from behind, but you can't block them. This is annoying when you have annoying archers on both sides.

 The merchants/ gold. The prob wasn't price; there's plenty of gold to be had. The problem is that there really isn't much to buy. It is pointless to buy armor/weapons, because they can all be found in chests/ dropped from enemies. Sometimes there'll be a tablet or ring available at that particular merchant (i.e. sunpearl scarab talisman). But mostly, merchants will be used to clean up your inventory/ buy the shabti gems & maps they sometimes have. There's no upgrading you gear or stats, or buying consumables, so you'll finish the game with tens of thousands of Ancient Egyptian dollarydoos. I finished with 74,315.


Overall/tips from a guy who beat the game
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall, Pharaonic is a nice little game. However, I would not describe this as a game worth playing through more than once unless you're an achievement hunter/ completionist sort.

-Combat is about stamina management and patience, not going berzerkity. You go berzikity, you'll have no stamina. No stamina means you can't dodge/ block. No dodge/block means you get whalloped.
-If you're having trouble with stamina management, use the Tablet of blessings. It remains useful throughout the whole game, and has a low ka cost.
-Don't get greedy with hits. Get greedy, and you'll get punished.
-Always leave yourself enough stamina to block/ dodge.
-Generally, it is most stamina efficient to dodge in place instead of forward roll/ back step/ block.
-Generally the great shields that block 90-something % of damage are better than the ones that block 100%. This is because they have higher swiftness.
-It is a good idea to have your weapon/armor be the opposite weight class. This is beacuse of how stamina works. Stamina pool = (Base Stamina - Total Armor Weight). Heavy weapons are stamina costly, even with investment into the skill. Doesn't go well with heavy armor.
-Invest your shabti gems wisely; there is a limited amount and there is no respec.
-There's a guide detailing where to find shabti gems and fixed treasure locations. Use it to avoid wasting money at merchants.
-There's no lvl 5 gear. Lvl 5 skills exist to get the bonuses for lvl 4 gear.
-If there are traps in the 'arenas', use them to your advantage.
- Don't let yourself get surrounded. You get enemies on both sides, get outta there.
